title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 7: Transparency, the Key to Sound Judgments
keywords: Transparency, the Key to Sound Judgments
primary_topics: Chapter 7 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- panel remarks by CJP, delivered from the standpoint of a country without jury trials, on how courts in an adversarial no-jury system acquire the information on which judgments rest and why transparency in that process is what makes the judgments acceptable.

He catalogued the six sources of information available to a judge and defended cross-examination as the main tool for filtering truth, while noting that judges must start with a clean slate and may not use prior knowledge of a case's specific facts.

He argued that because of the limits inherent in this method, a legal truth may not be the same as a scientific truth, and that acceptance of a judgment therefore turns on the transparency with which the court shows how it found the facts, applied the law and reached its conclusion.

Applying this to the hypothetical case before the panel, he took the position that the parties' privacy rights in genetic information, though real, were effectively waived by the suits they themselves filed, and that the public-interest elements of those cases argued overwhelmingly for opening every aspect of them to public scrutiny.
sub_topics: The opening caveat that, unlike Justice Thomas Fitzgerald of the Supreme Court of Illinois and Judge Sarah Evans Barker of the US District Court of Indiana, he comes from a country that does not observe jury trials -- a position he shares with Judge Amadeo Santosuosso of Milan.

The six sources of information for a judgment in an adversarial system: the pleadings; admissions in pleadings, pretrial or discovery; issues and questions raised in the proceedings; testimonial and documentary evidence at trial; oral or written arguments; and the litigants' citation of authorities.

Cross-examination as the essential weapon for testing a witness -- even an expert witness -- on credibility, observation, recollection, predilection and ability to state the truth, until science supplies something more reliable.

What is expected of judges themselves: knowledge of the law, logical and coherent reasoning, oral and written communication, and a more than passing knowledge of the humanities, economics, physics, medicine, religion, philosophy, mathematics and the sciences.

The clean-slate rule: judges are not supposed to have prior knowledge of a case's specific facts and, even if they do, are barred from using it; they must be objective and independent and rely solely on information brought forth at trial under the rules on evidence.

The anatomy of a judgment: it must state the facts culled from the evidence, the issues resolved and the laws on which it is anchored, and then present its conclusions and awards in clear language and lawyerly logic.
The gap between legal and scientific truth, which arises because scientists are not restricted by the legal norms and due process requirements that bind judges.
Transparency defined: enabling litigants and the general public to know how courts handle cases and how they arrive at decisions, and, for the individual, requiring informed consent at all times.

The countervailing duty: cases must still be decided according to law and reason, and won or lost on reasoned arguments from legal principles and precedents rather than popular palatability, accommodation, friendship or pecuniary consideration.

The dependence of courts on public faith: without popular support they become useless, since they cannot enforce their own pronouncements, command the army or the police or the raging mob, or grease political patronage.

The distinction between the shifting winds of public emotion and long-term institutional trust: critics may rant against particular decisions, but transparency earns residual esteem in which even level-headed critics concede the courts' good faith, wisdom, probity and diligence.

Why this matters more in developing countries: residual public trust is often presumed in advanced liberal democracies with mature judiciaries, but in evolving judicial traditions it becomes the litmus test of judicial independence and effectiveness and the very core of good governance.

His evidentiary posture: advocacy of the liberal acceptance of evidence subject to relevance and materiality, especially where expert evidence conflicts, leaving credibility and weight to the judge's discretion and wisdom.

The hypothetical case: Signora Francesca's privacy rights under national constitutions, laws and international conventions against undue exposure of genetic predisposition to disease, psychological disorders or negative behavioral tendencies, which could bring employment discrimination, insurance refusal or public ridicule.

Why he found those rights waived: the criminal suit in Milan against Alfredo, the civil damages and personal injury actions in Italy, and the patent invalidation actions in India, Australia and the U.S. -- since defendants cannot defend themselves in a public trial if barred by the plaintiffs' avowal of privacy.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced panel remarks in which Justice Panganiban spoke from the standpoint of a country without jury trials, distinguishing himself from fellow panelists Justice Thomas Fitzgerald of the Supreme Court of Illinois and Judge Sarah Evans Barker of the US District Court of Indiana, and aligning himself with Judge Amadeo Santosuosso of Milan. He catalogued the six sources from which a judgment in an adversarial system draws its information -- the pleadings, admissions made in pleadings or at pretrial or discovery, the issues and questions raised in the proceedings, testimonial and documentary evidence, oral and written arguments, and the litigants' citation of authorities -- and maintained that until science offers something more reliable, cross-examination remains the main tool for filtering truth and the essential weapon for testing a witness, expert or not, on credibility, observation, recollection, predilection and ability to state the truth. Judges, he said, are expected to know the law, reason logically and communicate clearly, and to have more than a passing knowledge of the humanities and sciences, but must start with a clean slate: they may not use prior knowledge of a case's specific facts. A judgment must state the facts culled from the evidence, the issues resolved and the laws on which it is anchored. Because this method is bounded by due process requirements that do not bind scientists, he observed, a legal truth may not be the same as a scientific truth, and acceptance of the judgment therefore depends on the transparency with which the court shows its process. Courts, he argued, are effective only so long as they retain public faith, since they command neither army, police nor patronage; transparency earns the residual long-term trust that survives the shifting winds of public emotion, and in developing countries that trust becomes the litmus test of judicial independence and the core of good governance. He declared himself an advocate of the liberal acceptance of evidence subject to relevance and materiality, and concluded on the panel's hypothetical that Signora Francesca's genetic privacy rights had been effectively waived by the suits filed in Milan, Italy, India, Australia and the United States, with public interest favoring full scrutiny.
